519.title: The poets
519.hook: the surah's name, and the poets excepted who believe, do good and remember Allah (26:224–227)
519.howItsDone: Muslims across the world sing and recite devotional poetry, from Arabic odes praising the Prophet to nasheeds and qawwali, while scholars hold that the Qur'an itself is not poetry.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khafd al-janah, lowering the wing in gentleness. Your line was lower the wing.

In the Arabia the Prophet grew up in, the old histories describe the poet as no quiet figure with a notebook. A poet could be a weapon and a newspaper at once. A tribe's poet praised his own people and mocked their rivals, and a sharp line could travel from camp to camp and stick to a family's name. So when the Prophet began reciting the Qur'an, some opponents had a label ready: he's just a poet. Surah Ash-Shu'ara, named for the poets, ends by answering that.

The surah's last verses don't flatter the poets of that time. Those who go astray follow them. They wander in every valley, chasing any mood or theme, and they say what they don't do. Commentators read this as the answer to the label: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, they say, was not wandering, and did what he said. Elsewhere the Qur'an says plainly that it is not the word of a poet. Then, in the very last verse, a turn: except those who believe, and do good works, and remember God much, and defend themselves after they have been wronged. So the surah doesn't ban poetry. It sorts it: words that wander, and words that remember. The exception had faces. The Prophet had poets among his companions, Hassan ibn Thabit among them. A report in Bukhari says the Prophet asked Hassan to answer the Quraysh's satires in verse, and prayed that God support him with the Holy Spirit, which Muslims understand as the angel Jibril. Another hadith in Bukhari says some poetry is wisdom. Later, Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, a poet who had written against the Prophet, came and recited a famous ode, and tradition says the Prophet gave him his own cloak; scholars discuss the strength of that story's chains. From those beginnings grew a long tradition of praise poems for the Prophet, in Arabic and many other languages, sung at weddings and gatherings. The surah's test is simple: do the words remember God, and do the people saying them live them?

520.title: The ant's warning
520.hook: an ant warns the others to hide from Sulayman's army, and he smiles and prays in thanks (27:18–19)
520.howItsDone: Muslims recite Sulayman's prayer of thanks from 27:19, and many cite the Prophet's prohibition on killing ants and bees as part of Islamic care for animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the poets, and words that wander or remember. Your line was words that remember. Today, a new surah.

People, jinn and birds, all marching in ranks. That's Sulayman's army in Surah An-Naml, the Ant, the twenty-seventh: hosts gathered and set in order, moving across the land. And somewhere at ankle height, in a valley, one tiny creature sees it coming. It doesn't run for itself. It turns and calls to everyone else, before it's too late. The surah is named for that moment, and that one small voice.
screen: `AN ARMY OF PEOPLE, JINN AND BIRDS.`

segments.voice: Sulayman, the surah says, had been taught the speech of birds. So when the army reaches the Valley of the Ants, he hears this. Pickthall: "O ants! Enter your dwellings lest Solomon and his armies crush you, unperceiving." Notice that last word. The ant doesn't call the army cruel. She says they'll crush us without noticing: she gives a great king the benefit of the doubt while getting everyone out of the way. In Arabic, the ant is feminine, a namla, and the verbs follow. Then the king's reaction. Pickthall: "And (Solomon) smiled, laughing at her speech". No anger, no order to punish. Straight away he turns it into a prayer: my Lord, make me thankful for Your favor on me and my parents, and to do good that pleases Thee. A king hears an insect, and his first words are thanks. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ took small creatures seriously too. A hadith in Bukhari tells of an earlier prophet, stung by an ant, who had the whole colony burned, and God rebuked him: because one ant stung you, you burned a whole nation that glorified Me? And in Abu Dawud, the Prophet forbade killing four creatures: the ant first, then the bee, the hoopoe and a small bird of prey. The story turns the usual picture upside down. The power is all on one side, and the attention, the smile and the thanks go the other way.

521.title: The hoopoe's news
521.hook: a small bird brings Sulayman news of a queen who worships the sun (27:20–26)
521.howItsDone: Muslims read the hoopoe's story in Surah An-Naml as a lesson in listening carefully and verifying news, and the hoopoe is among the creatures a hadith says not to kill.

segments.voice: Yesterday: namla, the ant who warned her colony. Your line was he smiled at the ant.

Sulayman is inspecting the birds, one by one, like a commander walking a line of troops. And there's a gap. Why don't I see the hoopoe, he asks. Is it absent? The hoopoe is a striking little bird, cinnamon-colored, with a crest that fans open like a crown and wings barred black and white. Sulayman isn't pleased. He'll punish it severely, he says, unless it brings a clear excuse. Not long after, the hoopoe lands.

Its first words are astonishing, given who it's talking to. In the Arabic: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed. Pickthall renders the next words: "I come unto thee from Sheba with sure tidings." A bird the size of your hand tells the man who speaks to birds and commands jinn that it knows something he doesn't. Then it reports carefully, like a good scout. A woman rules the people of Saba', Sheba. She's been given something of everything, and she has a great throne. The hoopoe saw her and her people bowing to the sun instead of God, because Shaytan had made their deeds look fair to them. It even adds a short reflection of its own, about God who brings out what is hidden in the heavens and the earth. Now look at Sulayman. He doesn't wave the bird away because it's small, or punish it for speaking boldly. He doesn't simply believe it either: we shall see whether you have told the truth or are one of the liars. And he sends the hoopoe back with a letter. That's the shape of the scene: listen to the small voice, then check it. Some commentators tell a story that the hoopoe could sense water underground, and that the army relied on it. That's from later commentary, not the verse. The verse gives enough: a king who noticed one bird missing, and a bird who came back knowing something he didn't.

522.title: The Queen of Sheba
522.hook: Bilqis consults her council, tests Sulayman, and submits with him to the Lord of the worlds (27:29–44)
522.howItsDone: Muslims often cite the Queen of Sheba's council as an example of shura, consultation, and many pray istikhara, the prayer for guidance, before a big decision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hoopoe, a small bird with big news. Your line was the hoopoe knew.

A letter lands in a throne room in Sheba. Sulayman has sent the hoopoe with it, told to throw it down to them. The queen opens it before her nobles. It's from a foreign king, and it's short: it opens in the name of God, the Merciful, and tells her not to rise up in pride against him but to come to him in surrender. A letter like that could start a war by evening. Watch what this queen does instead.

First, she reads it to her council, calls it a noble letter, and quotes its opening. Pickthall: "Lo! it is from Solomon, and lo! it is: In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful". That's the bismillah, inside a surah's verse, in a queen's mouth. Then she consults: I decide nothing, she tells her chiefs, until you are present. They answer like soldiers: we have strength and great might, but the command is yours. She doesn't reach for the might. Kings, she says, when they enter a town, ruin it and humble its honored people. So she tests him instead, with a gift, and waits to see what comes back. Sulayman refuses it: what God has given me is better than what He has given you. Then she travels to him. Her throne has been brought there before her, disguised, and she's asked: is your throne like this? Her careful answer: it's as though it were the very one. Then she's led into a hall and, thinking the floor is a pool of water, she lifts her skirt. It's smooth glass. And she speaks the surah's climax. Pickthall: "I surrender with Solomon unto Allah, the Lord of the Worlds." With Solomon, not to him. The Qur'an never gives her name. Muslim tradition calls her Bilqis; the Hebrew Bible also tells of a Queen of Sheba who visited Solomon with hard questions. In An-Naml, what stands out is her method. She consulted, avoided war, tested, looked closely, and when she saw, she said so.

523.title: Who answers the distressed
523.hook: who answers the one in distress when he calls, and removes the evil (27:62)
523.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite 27:62 in times of trouble and call on God in their own words in du'a, believing that the prayer of the one in distress is heard.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bilqis, the queen who consulted before she acted. Your line was she thought it through.

The car skids on ice. The doctor walks in with a face that's too careful. In that second, before any thinking, some people who rarely pray hear themselves say please, God. Not a formal prayer. Just a call, with nothing else left to try. Near the end of An-Naml, a run of questions about the signs of God reaches exactly that moment.

The passage goes like a drumbeat. Who created the heavens and the earth, sent down rain and grew gardens with it? Is there a god beside God? Who made the earth a fixed place, ran rivers through it, set the mountains, and put a barrier between the two seas? Is there a god beside God? Then verse sixty-two: who answers the one in distress when he calls on Him, and removes the evil, and makes you successors on the earth? Is there a god beside God? The word for the distressed is al-mudtarr. The classical dictionaries give it the sense of being forced, driven into a corner: not just sad, but with no other options left. The verse doesn't say the righteous, or the one who prays perfectly. It says the cornered one, when he calls. Some commentators link it to another passage, where people in a storm at sea call on God sincerely and then, safe on land, forget. The call itself is heard. That's why the verse sits among the signs, with rain and rivers and mountains: being answered in a corner is offered as something people know from their own lives, as plain as weather. A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi names three prayers answered without doubt: of the one who is wronged, of the traveler, and of a parent. Muslim teachers add that being answered doesn't always mean getting exactly what was asked. In their reading, the verse promises that the call is heard.

524.title: A mother's empty heart
524.hook: Musa's mother's heart became empty, and Allah steadied it (28:10)
524.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Musa's mother in Al-Qasas as a picture of trust in God under fear, and many recite its promise, We will bring him back to you, in times of separation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-mudtarr, the cornered one whose call is heard. Your line was he answers the distressed. Today, a new surah.

Pharaoh is killing the newborn boys of the Children of Israel, and a mother has just had a son. By an inspiration from God, she's told to nurse him, and when she fears for him, to put him in a chest, as another surah tells it, and cast him into the river. Don't fear, don't grieve, the verse says: We will bring him back to you. So she sets her baby on moving water and lets go. Surah Al-Qasas, the Stories, the twenty-eighth, begins Musa's life with her. Then comes the next morning.

The Qur'an doesn't skip over what she felt. Pickthall: "And the heart of the mother of Moses became void". The Arabic is farigh: emptied out, vacant. Empty of what, commentators asked. Some said of everything except Musa; others, of patience, or of the calm she'd had the night before. She was about to give him away, the verse goes on, to blurt out that the child was hers, had God not strengthened her heart. The word there is rabatna, We tied: the verb for tying something fast so it doesn't drift. And the verse says why: so that she would be among the believers, those who trust. Notice what God doesn't do. He doesn't take the fear away. Her heart is still empty; He ties it so that it holds. Then she does something very practical. She tells Musa's sister, follow him. The girl watches from a distance as the child reaches Pharaoh's household. God had kept him from taking any wet nurse, so the sister steps forward: shall I show you a family who will look after him? So Musa comes home, fed at his own mother's breast, inside Pharaoh's household. The verse says it was so that her eye would be cooled and she wouldn't grieve, and so she would know God's promise is true. In this telling, faith isn't the absence of panic. It's a heart held steady while it's still afraid.

525.title: Walking with modesty
525.hook: one of the two women comes to him walking with modesty (28:25)
525.howItsDone: Muslims speak of haya' as a quality of character for both men and women, shown in speech, bearing and conduct, and many recite Musa's prayer from 28:24 in times of need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: farigh, a mother's emptied heart, tied steady. Your line was a heart held steady.

Musa is a grown man now, and on the run. He has fled Egypt alone and walked all the way to Madyan. At a well, shepherds are crowding their flocks in to drink. Standing back, holding their animals away, are two women. He asks what's wrong. They can't water until the shepherds leave, they say, and their father is a very old man. So Musa waters their flock, then sits in the shade, exhausted, with nothing, and prays. And someone comes walking toward him.
screen: `A MAN ON THE RUN, AT A WELL.`
`HE SITS IN THE SHADE AND PRAYS.`

segments.voice: His prayer is one line long. Pickthall: "My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me." No plan, no demand. And what's sent comes walking. Pickthall: "Then there came unto him one of the two women, walking shyly." The Arabic says she walked 'ala istihya', upon shyness. The classical dictionaries put that word under the same root as haya', today's word, and hayat, life; some classical scholars, Ibn al-Qayyim among them, drew the connection: haya' keeps a heart alive. The verse describes her modesty by the way she walks: not her clothes, which it doesn't mention, but her pace and bearing. And in the same verse she speaks clearly to a stranger: my father invites you, to pay you for watering for us. Modesty here isn't silence or shrinking. It's dignified and unhurried, and still says exactly what needs saying. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim calls haya' a branch of faith; another, in Bukhari, says it brings nothing but good. A companion described the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ as shyer than a young woman behind her curtain, so haya' in Islam was never only for women. This week was full of people who carry themselves well: poets who remember, a king who smiled at an ant, a bird who knew, a queen who thought it through, a cornered caller who was heard, a heart held steady. And today, a woman whose modesty is a walk.
screen: `I AM NEEDY OF WHATEVER GOOD.` · `SHE CAME WALKING SHYLY.` · `HAYA' AND HAYAT: MODESTY AND LIFE.` · `A WALK, AND A CLEAR VOICE.`

segments.voice: Notice your posture right now, shoulders, jaw, hands, and let them settle. Picture walking into the next room you'll enter at an even pace, head level, neither performing nor shrinking, and saying what you need simply, then stopping. If you pray, you can repeat Musa's words from the shade: my Lord, I need whatever good You send me.
Haya'. Modesty, shyness, a sense of dignity before God and people; in the hadith, a branch of faith that brings nothing but good. Today's word.
Your line: modesty is a walk. Dignity can be quiet and still speak clearly. That's the week, done.
